artiest/henry-minton.text:
Henry Minton was a tenor saxophonist and club owner in Harlem, New York. In 1938 he founded Minton's Playhouse, a jazz club on the first floor of the Cecil Hotel on West 118th Street. Before opening his club he had worked in the music world: he was the first Black delegate of the American Federation of Musicians Local 802 and, in the 1930s, manager of the Rhythm Club in Harlem, which Louis Armstrong, Fats Waller, James P. Johnson and Earl Hines often visited. That experience gave him a knowledge of the economic and artistic needs of jazz musicians in New York. He was also generous with food and loans, and that made his club a beloved place for musicians.

Minton introduced a standing jam-session policy. Thanks to his contacts at the union, musicians did not have to fear a fine for playing without pay, something the union officially forbade. Dizzy Gillespie recalled that the union's delegates followed musicians around and fined them, but that Minton's was somewhat immune. At the end of 1940 he brought in Teddy Hill as manager.

It was in those jam sessions in the early 1940s that Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, Kenny Clarke, Charlie Christian, Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie developed bebop. That made Minton's a key place for modern jazz. The club continued to flourish for about thirty years and closed in 1974.
artiest/henry-minton.listen: Listen to a bebop recording by Dizzy Gillespie or Thelonious Monk. Notice the fast tempo and how the soloists challenge one another, as in the jam sessions at Minton's.

artiest/henry-purcell.text: Henry Purcell was organist of Westminster Abbey and wrote music for the English court, the church and the London theatre. He combined French and Italian influences with an unerring feel for the sound of the English language. In his opera Dido and Aeneas, Dido sings her farewell over a chromatically descending bass line that keeps returning. He died at thirty-six and was buried in the Abbey, close to the organ.
artiest/henry-purcell.listen: Listen to the beginning of Dido's Lament and follow the bass line that sinks downward in small semitone steps and starts again and again.

artiest/henry-ragas.text:
Henry Ragas was an American jazz pianist, born on 2 November 1890 and died on 18 February 1919. He played piano in the Original Dixieland Jass Band, the first jazz band to make commercial recordings. That makes him the first jazz pianist to be captured on record, piano rolls aside. Because of the primitive recording equipment, his contribution is barely audible. He filled in the chords and played a bass line, and took no solos.

Between 1910 and 1913 Ragas gained experience as a solo pianist. In 1916 he travelled to Chicago with Johnny Stein's band and left that group to form the Original Dixieland Jass Band. He played on the band's first twenty-one recordings, including Bluin' the Blues, which he composed himself. He also wrote Lazy Daddy, Dixieland Jass Band One-Step, Clarinet Marmalade Blues and Reisenweber Rag.

He played on classics such as Livery Stable Blues, often regarded as the first jazz record, and Tiger Rag, one of the most recorded jazz tunes. Darktown Strutters' Ball from 1917 entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2006. Ragas died in the Spanish flu epidemic of 1919. J. Russel Robinson took his place.
artiest/henry-ragas.listen: Listen to Livery Stable Blues by the Original Dixieland Jass Band. Notice the animal noises from the horns and try to hear the piano underneath, which mostly plays chords and a bass line.

artiest/henry-threadgill.text:
Henry Threadgill is an American composer, saxophonist and flautist, born on 15 February 1944. He became known in the 1970s with groups that were rooted in jazz but used unusual line-ups and other genres. He studied piano, flute and composition at the American Conservatory of Music in Chicago. There he played in the Experimental Band, a forerunner of the AACM, led by Muhal Richard Abrams. In 1967 he joined the army and played in a rock band in Vietnam.

After his return he formed a trio with bassist Fred Hopkins and drummer Steve McCall that grew into Air. In New York he founded X-75, a nonet with four reed players, four bassists and a singer. In the 1980s came his Sextet, actually a septet, with two drummers, double bass, cello, trumpet and trombone alongside his alto saxophone and flute. The album You Know the Number is regarded as one of his most accessible. Further groups included Very Very Circus, Make a Move and Zooid.

In 2016 he won the Pulitzer Prize for Music with In for a Penny, In for a Pound. In 2023 his autobiography Easily Slip into Another World, written with Brent Hayes Edwards, was published. Threadgill is regarded as one of the most important composers to have shifted the boundary between jazz and contemporary classical music.
artiest/henry-threadgill.listen: Listen to Easily Slip Into Another World. Notice the unusual combination of instruments and how you are never sure which instrument carries the melody.

artiest/henryk-gorecki.text:
Henryk Górecki was a Polish composer of contemporary classical music. He was born in 1933 in Czernica, in the south of Poland, and studied in Rybnik and Katowice. There he later became a teacher and provost of the music academy. He had poor health from a leg disease in his youth. His mother died when he was two, and he dedicated many early works to her.

In the 1950s and 1960s he was known as a leading figure of the Polish avant-garde. His work was then dissonant and modernist, influenced by Webern, Nono, Stockhausen and Penderecki. In the mid-1970s he chose a simpler, religious minimalism. An example is the Symphony No. 3, nicknamed the Symphony of Sorrowful Songs, from 1976. The work consists of slow movements with soprano, in which short motifs return again and again.

Until the late 1980s hardly anyone outside Poland knew him. That changed in 1992, when a recording of the symphony with soprano Dawn Upshaw and conductor David Zinman became a worldwide success and sold more than a million copies, far more than a classical record by a twentieth-century composer usually achieves. Górecki himself did not want to repeat that success and went on his own way. He shows that quiet, slow music, too, can move a large audience.
artiest/henryk-gorecki.listen: Listen to the slow movement Lento e largo and notice how the music hardly moves forward. Hear how the soprano appears above the slowly swelling strings.

artiest/herbert-stothart.text: Herbert Stothart was born in Milwaukee in 1885 and came from Broadway, where he wrote and conducted operettas, including Rose-Marie (1924) together with Rudolf Friml. In 1929 he joined MGM and was its musical director there for years. The Rogue Song (1930), with the opera singer Lawrence Tibbett, was an early musical film in colour. Stothart worked in the style of late Romanticism: lots of strings, familiar melodies as quotation, and music that doubles the emotion of a scene. He wrote the score for Mutiny on the Bounty (1935). For The Wizard of Oz (1939) he wove Harold Arlen's songs into his orchestral music and won an Oscar. His work typifies the smooth studio sound of MGM.
artiest/herbert-stothart.listen: Notice how song melodies such as 'Over the Rainbow' return in the orchestra as themes that announce characters and places.

artiest/herbert-von-karajan.text:
Herbert von Karajan was an Austrian conductor, born Heribert Adolf Ernst Karajan on 5 April 1908 and died on 16 July 1989. His ancestors were of Greek descent. His great-great-grandfather Georg Karajan came from Kozani and moved to Vienna in 1767, and the addition von came from a title of nobility granted in 1792. Karajan made his debut at the Salzburg Festival, with the Wiener Philharmoniker and the Berliner Philharmoniker, and during the war conducted at the Staatsoper in Berlin. He was then a member of the Nazi Party, which made him controversial.

From the mid-1950s until his death he was a dominant figure in European classical music. He was principal conductor of the Berliner Philharmoniker for thirty-four years. His recordings from the 1950s include operas by Mozart and Wagner, the symphonies of Beethoven and Tchaikovsky, and works by Richard Strauss, such as Don Juan and Till Eulenspiegel. He made so many records that, by one estimate, he sold two hundred million copies.

Karajan is regarded as one of the greatest conductors of the twentieth century. Part of his influence came from the scale and visibility of his recordings. He made classical music into a product that lay next to pop music on the record shelves in the shop, and that makes him a figure who also fits into a history of pop.
artiest/herbert-von-karajan.listen: Listen to Don Juan by Richard Strauss in a recording by Karajan. Notice the sheen of the orchestra and how the conductor makes the piece sound like one long, driving line.

artiest/herbie-hancock.text: Herbie Hancock, from Chicago, played a Mozart concerto with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra at the age of eleven. In jazz he named Bill Evans as an important influence on his harmony. His first album Takin' Off (1962) contained Watermelon Man, which became a hit. From 1963 to 1968 he played in Miles Davis's second quintet. For Blue Note he recorded Maiden Voyage, a modal album about the sea. In the 1970s he went electric: Head Hunters (1973) brought jazz and funk together. In 1983 he had a hit with Rockit, with scratches by a DJ. Hancock kept on using new technology.
artiest/herbie-hancock.listen: Notice the piano chords: open and floating, never fully resolved.

artiest/herbie-nichols.text:
Herbie Nichols was an American jazz pianist and composer, born on 3 January 1919 in San Juan Hill in Manhattan, to parents from St. Kitts and Trinidad. He grew up in Harlem. His first known work was in 1937 with the Royal Barons. A few years later he played at Minton's Playhouse, but the competitive atmosphere did not suit him. He did become friends with Thelonious Monk. In 1941 he joined the army.

After the war he played in all kinds of line-ups, often Dixieland to earn a living, while he would rather have made adventurous jazz. Recognition came when Mary Lou Williams recorded a few of his songs in 1952. Alfred Lion of Blue Note signed him only in 1955 and 1956, and some of those recordings were not released until the 1980s. His song Serenade was given lyrics and, as Lady Sings the Blues, became associated with Billie Holiday. In 1957 he made his last album as a leader for Bethlehem Records.

Nichols combined bebop, Dixieland and Caribbean music with harmonies from Erik Satie and Béla Bartók. He was almost unknown during his lifetime and died in 1963, aged forty-four, of leukaemia. Later Roswell Rudd, Steve Lacy and the Herbie Nichols Project championed his music, and he is now regarded as one of the most idiosyncratic jazz composers.
artiest/herbie-nichols.listen: Listen to Lady Sings the Blues, originally Nichols's Serenade. Notice how the melody is bluesy and yet unusual in its construction.

artiest/herman-brood.text:
Herman Brood was a Dutch singer, pianist, painter and actor, born in 1946 in Zwolle. He had piano lessons at a young age and from 1964 played in the beat group The Moans. He was then allowed to play with Cuby and the Blizzards, but the record company had him thrown out of the band when it emerged that he used drugs. Years of short-lived jobs followed, including with Vitesse, and periods in prison.

In 1976 Brood started his own group, Herman Brood & His Wild Romance. The band first played in cafés and clubs in Groningen and in 1977 released the album Street. The breakthrough came with Shpritsz (1978), with songs such as Dope Sucks, Rock & Roll Junkie and the hit Saturday Night. It was raw rock 'n' roll with piano, guitars and saxophone, and Brood sang in English. In 1979 he starred with Nina Hagen in the film Cha Cha and tried to conquer America. A new recording of Saturday Night entered the Billboard Hot 100, but the big breakthrough failed to come. Later he had another hit with Als je wint, together with Henny Vrienten.

Brood became as well known for his candid statements about sex and drugs as for his music. He was regarded as the only true Dutch rock 'n' roll star. Later he became a successful painter of colourful pop art. In 2001 he took his own life in Amsterdam. His version of My Way then spent three weeks at number 1.
artiest/herman-brood.listen: Listen to Saturday Night (1978) by Herman Brood & His Wild Romance. Notice Brood's rolling piano playing and how the band sounds like a rock 'n' roll group from the pub, with English lyrics.

artiest/herman-hupfeld.text:
Herman Hupfeld was an American songwriter, born on 18 February 1894 in Montclair, New Jersey, and died on 8 June 1951. His mother was a church organist. At the age of nine he went to study violin in Germany. He graduated from high school in Montclair in 1915, joined the Navy in the First World War and then began as a songwriter. During the Second World War he performed in camps and hospitals.

Hupfeld never wrote a complete Broadway score, but was known as someone who could write a song for a particular scene in a show. His best-known song is As Time Goes By, for which he wrote both lyrics and music. The song was intended for the 1931 show Everybody's Welcome, which ran for 139 performances, and then became a modest hit. Max Steiner did not want it in Casablanca, the 1942 film, but it was used in it anyway and became world-famous through it. Bing Crosby recorded it in 1943. Other songs of his are Sing Something Simple and When Yuba Plays the Rumba on the Tuba. Goopy Geer became the basis for a Merrie Melodies cartoon.

Hupfeld rarely performed, never married and lived with his mother until his death. That a single song from the American theatre song tradition has become so strongly tied to one film is part of his legacy.
artiest/herman-hupfeld.listen: Listen to As Time Goes By in the version from Casablanca. Notice the simple melody and the lyrics about things that remain, even when the world changes.

artiest/hesperion-xxi.text:
Hespèrion XXI is an international early-music ensemble. The group was founded in Basel in 1974 as Hespèrion XX by the Catalan leader Jordi Savall, who plays string instruments, especially the viola da gamba, his wife, the soprano Montserrat Figueras, Lorenzo Alpert, flute and percussion, and Hopkinson Smith, plucked instruments. At the beginning of the twenty-first century the name changed to Hespèrion XXI. The name comes from a Greek word for the peoples of the Italian and Iberian peninsulas.

The ensemble is known for its research into early music, especially the Spanish music of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The first recordings from 1976 present music from Christian and Jewish Spain, with villancicos and Sephardic romances. Cansós de Trobairitz from 1978, with songs by Catalan troubadours, and Libre vermell de Montserrat from 1979, a fourteenth-century pilgrims' songbook, followed. The group also played English consort music by Jenkins, Locke and Purcell, among others.

The performances stand out for their generous improvisation around the melodic and rhythmic basis of the old pieces, which gives a great emotional immediacy. The group has won the Edison Prize, the Grand Prix du Disque of the Académie Charles Cros and the Diapason d'Or, among other awards. Hespèrion shows that early music can be vivid for a contemporary listener.
artiest/hesperion-xxi.listen: Listen to Libre vermell de Montserrat. Notice the simple melodies and the rhythm of the percussionists, and how the musicians improvise freely around them.

artiest/het-goede-doel.text:
Het Goede Doel was a pop group from Utrecht, founded in 1979 by Henk Temming and Sander van Herk. Henk Westbroek joined that same year. The core became the duo of Westbroek and Temming, who wrote the songs together. Het Goede Doel belongs to the wave of bands that made Dutch-language pop big in the early 1980s, alongside Doe Maar, Toontje Lager and the Frank Boeijen Groep, among others.

Het Goede Doel combined the cool, electronic sound of the early 1980s with lyrics in Dutch. In 1982 the single Gijzelaar was boycotted by the broadcaster TROS. In October of that year België (Is er leven op Pluto...?) was released, produced by Robin Freeman. In the song someone wants to leave the Netherlands, but Pluto and other countries offer no solution; only in the last verse does the title appear. The single reached number 4 in the Top 40. The debut album België (1982) went platinum. In 1983 came Vriendschap, which reached number 3 in the Nationale Hitparade, and Eenvoud.

Around 1991 the group broke up. Reunions followed in 2001 and from 2007 to 2015. Westbroek later became a radio presenter at 3FM, a politician for Leefbaar Utrecht and a solo artist. Temming continued as a producer and songwriter. In 2012 Scala & Kolacny Brothers recorded a version of België of their own.
artiest/het-goede-doel.listen: België (1982) lasts well over six minutes. Notice the cool synthesizer sound beneath lyrics full of questions that seem to be about nothing, and wait for the last verse: only there does the word that gives the song its title appear.

artiest/hikaru-utada.text:
Hikaru Utada is a Japanese-American singer, songwriter and producer. Utada was born in New York in 1983 to Japanese parents: the producer Teruzane Utada and the enka singer Keiko Fuji. At the age of ten Utada wrote the first songs and at eleven the family moved to Tokyo. Under the name Cubic U, the English-language debut album Precious was released in 1998.

The breakthrough came a year later with First Love (1999), the first Japanese-language album. It leaned on R&B and dance pop and became the best-selling album in Japanese history. The single Automatic, which had already come out in 1998, was one of the hits from that album. Distance (2001) and Deep River (2002) followed, with Hikari and Sakura Drops among others, and later Exodus (2004), Ultra Blue (2006) and Heart Station (2008). After a long break Utada returned with the acoustic albums Fantôme (2016) and Hatsukoi (2018), and in 2022 with Bad Mode. Internationally Utada is best known for the theme song Simple and Clean for the game series Kingdom Hearts.

The music combines American R&B with Japanese pop and styles such as folk. The Japan Times called Utada the most influential artist of the decade for Japan. Utada was one of the first well-known Japanese people to identify as non-binary. It is an example of how a Japanese artist could connect the pop music of their own country with international R&B.
artiest/hikaru-utada.listen: Listen to Automatic and notice the rhythm and the singing style: can you hear how R&B influences colour the Japanese pop?

artiest/hilary-summers.text:
Hilary Summers is a Welsh lyric contralto. She studied at the University of Reading, the Royal Academy of Music and the National Opera Studio in London. Her voice is low and warm, a rare voice type that in opera often sings male roles, witches and other unusual characters.

She sings on soundtracks, including those of The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers, The Libertine and The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. She has created roles for the composers Péter Eötvös and Elliott Carter, and has a close collaboration with Michael Nyman. In his opera Facing Goya she sang the lead role of the Art Banker. In 2000 she sang the role of Mars in the first modern revival of Giovanni Legrenzi's La divisione del mondo at the Schwetzingen festival. In 2008 she sang the Sorceress in Dido and Aeneas at the Opéra-Comique, under William Christie.

Her discography runs from the Baroque to the present. On Chandos there are Handel's Partenope and Semele, and there are further recordings of Lotario, Flavio, Serse and Israel in Ägypten. In this way she moves between early opera and contemporary music, and also on the border between classical and film music.
artiest/hilary-summers.listen: Listen to an aria by Handel from Serse or Semele. Notice the low, dark colour of her voice and how nimbly she nevertheless sings the ornaments.

artiest/hildegard-von-bingen.text: Hildegard von Bingen was abbess of the convent of Rupertsberg on the Rhine, and also a writer, healer and visionary. For her sisters she wrote the words and music of more than seventy chants, with melodies that reach much higher and wider than ordinary Gregorian chant. Her Ordo Virtutum of around 1151 is a sung play in which the virtues fight for a human soul. She is one of the first composers of whom we know both the name and the work.
artiest/hildegard-von-bingen.listen: Listen to the single voice in Columba aspexit and hear how the melody shoots upward in large leaps, much further than in ordinary Gregorian chant.

artiest/hildur-gu-nadottir.text: Hildur Guðnadóttir was born in Reykjavík in 1982 and is a cellist. She played in experimental bands and for years worked with Jóhann Jóhannsson, including on Sicario (2015). She then wrote Sicario: Day of the Soldado (2018) herself. Her cello, often electronically processed, is central to her music. For the series Chernobyl (2019) she used only sounds that she recorded in a decommissioned nuclear power plant in Lithuania, and transformed them into music. For Joker (2019) she wrote music before filming began, so that the actor Joaquin Phoenix could move to it. She won an Oscar for it. Tár (2022) also bears her stamp.
artiest/hildur-gu-nadottir.listen: Listen to the cello that scrapes and creaks, and to sounds from the real world that are part of the music as rhythm and tone colour.

artiest/hilliard-ensemble.text:
The Hilliard Ensemble was a British male vocal quartet, founded in 1974 and named after the Elizabethan miniature painter Nicholas Hilliard. The founders were Paul Hillier, Errol Girdlestone, Paul Elliott and David James. The line-up was flexible until Hillier left in 1990. After that David James, Rogers Covey-Crump, John Potter and Gordon Jones formed the core, with Potter replaced by Steven Harrold in 1998. In 2014 the group ceased to exist.

The quartet sang mainly music from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance, but also contemporary works. It often worked with the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt and included pieces by John Cage, Gavin Bryars, Giya Kancheli and Heinz Holliger in its concerts. In the 1980s an extensive series of recordings appeared on EMI, and after that mainly on the label ECM. In 1994, when interest in Gregorian chant was at its height, Officium was released, a unique collaboration with the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek. It became one of the best-selling ECM releases and reached the charts in several European countries. The sequel Mnemosyne followed in 1999 and Officium Novum in 2010.

Of Pérotin, the composer from Paris around 1200, the quartet sang Viderunt omnes and Sederunt principes. This is polyphonic music from the time of the cathedral of Notre-Dame, in which long notes in the low voices are crowned by melodic lines. The ensemble made medieval sounds accessible to a wide audience.
artiest/hilliard-ensemble.listen: Listen to Viderunt omnes by Pérotin. Notice how the low voices hold very long notes while the higher voices move above them.

artiest/hilliard-ensemble-en-paul-hillie.text:
The Hilliard Ensemble was a British male vocal quartet that originally devoted itself to early music. The group is named after the Elizabethan miniature painter Nicholas Hilliard. It was founded in 1974 by Paul Hillier, David James and Paul Elliott, among others, and ceased to exist in 2014 after forty-one years, with a final concert at the Wigmore Hall in London. Hillier, one of the founders, left the group in 1990.

The repertoire lay mainly in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. In the 1980s a broad series of recordings appeared on the label EMI Reflexe, with works by Dunstable, Josquin, Palestrina and Ockeghem, among others, including a performance of the latter's Requiem and Missa Mi-Mi in 1984. Later the group recorded mainly for ECM. The ensemble also sang contemporary music, much by Arvo Pärt, and works by John Cage and Heinz Holliger, among others.

In 1994 Officium was released, a recording with the Norwegian saxophonist Jan Garbarek, in which the singers combined Gregorian chant and early polyphony with jazzy saxophone sounds. The album became one of ECM's best-selling releases and entered the pop charts in several European countries. In this way the quartet brought very old music to an audience that would otherwise never have listened to such choral music. The pure, transparent ensemble singing of four voices became a model for later early-music ensembles.
artiest/hilliard-ensemble-en-paul-hillie.listen: Listen to the Kyrie from Ockeghem's Missa prolationum and follow how the voices chase each other in long, undulating lines. Try to hear that each voice sings its own melody.

artiest/hirini-melbourne.text:
Hirini Melbourne, also known as Sid, was a Māori composer, singer, teacher, poet and writer. He was born on 21 July 1949 in Te Urewera, of the Ngāi Tūhoe and Ngāti Kahungunu tribes, and died on 6 January 2003. He is known for his contribution to the development of Māori music and the revival of Māori culture. He became a teacher, but did not enjoy it, and became an editor of Māori texts at the Ministry of Education in Wellington. From 1978 he worked at the University of Waikato, where he became a professor and dean of the School of Māori and Pacific Development.

Melbourne began writing waiata, songs, early on, often with Māori proverbs. His song E Kui e Koro contains the saying that you should have a second home in case the first fails. He also played the traditional instruments, ngā taonga pūoro. In 1985 he met the ethnomusicologist Richard Nunns. Together they performed on marae, in schools, galleries and concerts, and gathered knowledge about the instruments. Their recordings Toiapiapi from 1991, Te Kū Te Whē from 1994 and Te Hekenga-ā-rangi from 2003 have breathed new life into the use of these instruments. He recorded the last album weeks before his death.

Melbourne was a member of the protest group Nga Tamatoa. Many of his songs have been sung by others, including Hinewehi Mohi, Moana Maniapoto and the Topp Twins. He received a royal honour from New Zealand for his services to Māori music.
artiest/hirini-melbourne.listen: Listen to Toiapiapi. Notice the soft sounds of the old instruments, such as flutes of bone and wood, and how they sound at once like natural sound and like music.

artiest/hirokazu-tanaka.text:
Hirokazu Tanaka, nicknamed Hip or Chip Tanaka, is a Japanese musician, composer and sound designer, born on 13 December 1957. He is regarded as a pioneer of chiptune. His mother was a teacher and had him take piano lessons. At secondary school he played in a cover band of the Beatles and Elton John, and in his teens in a reggae band that twice opened for Sly and Robbie. His love of reggae has never gone away.

In 1980, after studying electrical engineering, he started at Nintendo as a sound designer. He made the music for Space Firebird and built a new sound chip for it. In Donkey Kong he supplied the sounds for Mario's steps and jumps, with subtle variations. He was one of Nintendo's in-house composers in the 8- and 16-bit era. His credits include Metroid, Kid Icarus, Super Mario Land, Tetris, Mother, Dr. Mario and EarthBound. He also helped design and program the audio of the Famicom and the Game Boy, as well as the NES Zapper, the Game Boy Camera and the Game Boy Printer. From 2001 to 2023 he was president of Creatures Inc.

Tanaka showed that with a few simple sound channels you can make a melody that carries an entire game. For a generation of listeners his work was the first encounter with electronic pop music, and his sound lives on in today's chiptune.
artiest/hirokazu-tanaka.listen: Listen to the music of Metroid or Super Metroid. Notice how few sound channels there are and how atmospheric the melody and the bass nevertheless sound.

artiest/hiromi.text: Hiromi Uehara was born in Hamamatsu in 1979 and had piano lessons as a child. At seventeen she met Chick Corea in Tokyo, who had her sit in at his concert the next day. She studied at Berklee in Boston, where the pianist Ahmad Jamal noticed her. Her debut Another Mind (2003) was released on the label Telarc. Hiromi plays at great speed and mixes jazz with rock, classical music and electronic sounds. With Chick Corea she made the duet album Duet (2008), and she played in the trio of bassist Stanley Clarke. From 2011 she worked with bassist Anthony Jackson and drummer Simon Phillips in The Trio Project.
artiest/hiromi.listen: Listen to the fast runs and the sudden changes of style.

artiest/hiroshi-miyagawa.text:
Hiroshi Miyagawa is a Japanese composer best known for the music of Space Battleship Yamato, also called Star Blazers in the West. He worked for the producer Yoshinobu Nishizaki, whose company West Cape Corporation made the Yamato series.

His music for the series was released on many records, including as Symphonic Suite Yamato in 1977 and later as collections of background music for the various parts and films, such as Yamato yo Towa ni and Space Battleship Yamato III. In 1985 he wrote the music for the science-fiction film Odin: Photon Sailer Starlight, directed by Toshio Masuda, who had also worked on Yamato.

Miyagawa wrote orchestral music for animation, with big melodies and a symphonic sound that suits the space adventures. In this way he belongs to the composers who gave Japanese animation a sound of its own. His themes are made to carry stories of space travel, courage and loss, and they stay with the viewer after the film has ended.
artiest/hiroshi-miyagawa.listen: Listen to Symphonic Suite Yamato. Notice the big orchestral themes and how they sound both rugged and melodious.

artiest/hoketus.text:
Hoketus was an amplified music ensemble that the Dutch composer Louis Andriessen founded in 1976. The group came together to perform his minimalist composition Hoketus, but continued to exist and also played works by other composers, many of whom came from within the group itself. The ensemble ceased in 1987.

The line-up was radical. There were two equal groups of instruments: two pianos, two Fender Rhodes electric pianos, two sets of panpipes, two saxophones, two electric bass guitars and two percussionists. The group saw itself as a collective and drew up rules that together almost formed a manifesto. The ensemble always played loudly amplified, and the two groups stood as far apart as possible on stage. Personal expression was not allowed. Melodies arose only from the interlocking of single notes or chords, played alternately by the two groups, using the medieval technique of the hocket, from which the group took its name.

The preference was for work that was heavy, loud, dissonant and hard, under the influence of both hard rock and Igor Stravinsky, one of Andriessen's favourite composers. Besides Andriessen, composers including Diderik Wagenaar, Cornelis de Bondt, Michael Nyman, Huib Emmer, Cees van Zeeland, Klas Torstensson and Gene Carl wrote for Hoketus. In 1989 the group Icebreaker was formed in York with a similar line-up, and it continues to play the Hoketus repertoire.
artiest/hoketus.listen: Listen to Hoketus by Louis Andriessen. Notice how neither group plays a melody, but the notes leap back and forth between the two sides until a single line emerges after all.

artiest/holland-dozier-holland.text:
Holland-Dozier-Holland was the songwriting and production team of Lamont Dozier and the brothers Brian and Eddie Holland. All three began as performers. Eddie Holland was already working with Berry Gordy before the founding of Motown and had a hit with Jamie in 1962. Brian Holland co-wrote Please Mr. Postman for The Marvelettes, and Dozier made records for small labels. In 1962 they began writing together, and they soon noticed that they preferred writing and producing to performing themselves.

Dozier and Brian Holland wrote the music and produced, while Eddie Holland wrote the lyrics and the vocal arrangements. From 1962 to 1967 they made 25 number 1 hits at Motown. Among them were Heat Wave for Martha and the Vandellas, How Sweet It Is (To Be Loved by You) for Marvin Gaye and Reach Out I'll Be There for The Four Tops. For The Supremes they wrote ten of their twelve American number 1s, such as Baby Love, Stop! In the Name of Love and You Keep Me Hangin' On.

Together with Motown's regular session musicians and backing singers they defined the typical Motown sound. In 1967 they fell out with Gordy over money and royalties, and in early 1968 they left. They started their own labels Invictus and Hot Wax, but because of a years-long lawsuit they were not allowed to put their own names on their songs. In 1973 Dozier left. In 1990 the trio was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/holland-dozier-holland.listen: Listen to You Keep Me Hangin' On by The Supremes (1966). Notice the guitar that keeps ticking like Morse code and how Diana Ross sings the despair of the lyrics more and more urgently.

artiest/hongaarse-en-transsylvaanse-volk.text:
This name refers to Hungarian and Transylvanian folk musicians who were recorded in the twentieth century, among others by researchers who wanted to capture village music. They are not famous names, but players and singers from regions where Hungarian was spoken, from the Hungarian lowlands to Romanian Transylvania. Their music was handed down from generation to generation, often without sheet music.

The recording Verbunkos from 1964 belongs to a well-known Hungarian musical form. Verbunkos was originally the music of army recruitment in the eighteenth century. A typical verbunkos alternates slow, proud passages with fast, fiery ones. Often violins are the leaders, frequently with an accompaniment of a cimbalom and bass. Later these melodies became part of Hungarian classical music, including in the work of Franz Liszt and Johannes Brahms.

For pop history this kind of folk music is important as a source. Composers such as Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály travelled through Hungary and Transylvania in the early twentieth century to write down and record songs and dances, and drew inspiration from them. In this way this music shows that much of what we call modern music grew out of the rhythms, the scales and the sense of improvisation of rural players.
artiest/hongaarse-en-transsylvaanse-volk.listen: Listen to Verbunkos and notice the changes of tempo and character: where does the music sound slow and dignified, and where does it speed up and turn wild?

artiest/hooverphonic.text:
Hooverphonic is a Belgian band founded in 1995. The group was first called Hoover, but the name was changed because other bands were already using it. The permanent core consists of bassist and programmer Alex Callier and guitarist Raymond Geerts. Around them the female singers changed: Liesje Sadonius sang on the debut, then came Geike Arnaert, later Noémie Wolfs and Luka Cruysberghs, and in 2020 Arnaert returned.

The debut A New Stereophonic Sound Spectacular (1996) brought trip hop full of breakbeats and samples. The track 2Wicky, with a riff from Isaac Hayes's Walk On By, appeared in the film Stealing Beauty and gave the group international fame. On Blue Wonder Power Milk (1998), with the eighteen-year-old Arnaert, the music sounded warmer, with strings and more classical song forms. The Magnificent Tree (2000) produced Mad About You and brought the international breakthrough. Then followed the concept album Hooverphonic presents Jackie Cane (2002), an orchestral period and the psychedelic The President of the LSD Golf Club (2007).

Hooverphonic began as trip hop but grew into a band that mixes electronics, pop, rock and orchestra. The group is one of the few acts equally well known in Flanders and Wallonia. In 2001 they were the first Belgian band to close Rock Werchter, and in 2021 they sang The Wrong Place at the Eurovision Song Contest. Arnaert's voice, which was later also heard outside the band, remained for many listeners the sound of the group.
artiest/hooverphonic.listen: Listen to Mad About You (2000). Notice the strings that carry the song and how Geike Arnaert's calm, dreamy voice floats above them.

artiest/horace-silver.text: Pianist Horace Silver grew up in Norwalk, Connecticut; his father came from Cape Verde. As a young pianist he admired Bud Powell. Stan Getz took him into his band in 1950. Together with Art Blakey, Silver laid the foundation for the Jazz Messengers; after that he led a quintet of his own at Blue Note for years. He wrote short, catchy themes with influences from gospel, blues and Latin music, such as The Preacher and Señor Blues. His playing was funky and rhythmic, with short motifs. Song for My Father (1964) he dedicated to his father; the piano riff at the start was later borrowed by Steely Dan. Silver was one of the most important composers of hard bop.
artiest/horace-silver.listen: Notice the short, rhythmic piano figures beneath the theme.

artiest/hossein-alizadeh.text:
Hossein Alizadeh is an Iranian musician, composer and researcher, and a leading player of the tar, the shurangiz and the setar. He was born in Tehran in 1951. As a teenager he went to a conservatoire, then studied composition and performance at the University of Tehran. After the Iranian revolution he continued his studies in composition and musicology in Berlin.

Alizadeh performed with national orchestras of Iran and with ensembles such as the Aref Ensemble, the Shayda Ensemble and Masters of Persian Music. His first professional performance in Europe was with the orchestra of the Béjart Ballet, in the ballet Golestan. He worked with singers and players such as Shahram Nazeri, Mohammad-Reza Shajarian and Jivan Gasparyan. With Gasparyan he made the album Endless Vision, which received a Grammy nomination in 2007. Other albums include Faryad, Sallaneh, Half Moon and Ode To Flowers. He also developed new instruments, such as the sallaneh and the shoor-angiz, derived from the ancient Persian lute barbat.

His music stands in the tradition of the radif, the body of melodic models of classical Persian music, but gives it a contemporary form. He is regarded as an important innovator who has brought Persian music to a large international audience. In 2014 he refused the French Légion d'honneur.
artiest/hossein-alizadeh.listen: Listen to Setar Improvisation and notice how soft and precise the strings sound. Try to hear how a short melodic figure is repeated and extended again and again, without a fixed rhythm.

artiest/hot-butter.text:
Hot Butter was an American studio group from New York, active from 1971. The linchpin was keyboard player Stan Free, a trained jazz pianist who had previously played in Gershon Kingsley's First Moog Quartet. Kingsley had written Popcorn in 1969, a short instrumental piece for the Moog. In 1972 Free recorded it again with Hot Butter. That version became a worldwide hit and brought the sound of the synthesizer into the charts of half of Europe.

Popcorn lasts two and a half minutes. The Moog plays a bouncy melody of short, clipped notes, one note at a time. Underneath, drums, bass and guitar play like an ordinary pop band. The single was released in July 1972 in the United States on Musicor and reached number 1 in the Netherlands, West Germany, France, Switzerland and Australia, among other countries. In England it reached number 5, in the United States number 9. In France and Switzerland it was the best-selling single of 1972. The group then also recorded Apache and Tequila with the Moog.

Popcorn kept coming back. Jean-Michel Jarre recorded a version of his own under a pseudonym in 1972 and drew inspiration from it for Oxygène (Part IV) (1976). Aphex Twin made a techno version of it in 1992 as Caustic Window, and in 2005 the Crazy Frog version spent seven weeks at number 1 in France. The song shows how the synthesizer entered pop: first as a cheerful sound on top of an ordinary band, later, with Kraftwerk and the synth-pop of the 1980s, as the band itself.
artiest/hot-butter.listen: In Popcorn, listen to the Moog: it never plays a chord, only single notes one after another, because the synthesizer was monophonic. Because of the short, clipped attack, each note sounds like a popping kernel of corn, while drums and guitar simply carry on as in any pop single.

artiest/hot-five.text:
The Hot Five was the first band with which trumpeter Louis Armstrong recorded under his own name. The group came into being in 1925 in Chicago at the suggestion of Richard M. Jones of the Okeh label, and all the records were made in Okeh's studio. It was mainly a studio band: as the Hot Five the group performed live only twice. The first line-up consisted of Armstrong's wife Lil Hardin Armstrong on piano and three New Orleans musicians he already knew: Kid Ory on trombone, Johnny Dodds on clarinet and Johnny St. Cyr on banjo and guitar.

In November 1925 the first tracks were recorded, including Gut Bucket Blues. In 1926 came Cornet Chop Suey, Muskrat Ramble and Heebie Jeebies, with Armstrong's famous scat singing, which made him a well-known name in Chicago. At the end of 1927 came Struttin' with Some Barbecue and Hotter Than That. In 1928 Armstrong replaced all the other musicians with members of Carroll Dickerson's orchestra, including pianist Earl Hines. This second Hot Five played more written-out arrangements and recorded West End Blues and Weather Bird, among others.

The Hot Five played in the line-up of an ordinary New Orleans band: trumpet, clarinet and trombone with a rhythm section. In that style the horns played the melody together in collective improvisation. With the Hot Five the trumpet increasingly got room for a solo. In those solos Armstrong laid the foundation for the language of jazz improvisation, and with that the centre of gravity of the group shifted to the soloist.
artiest/hot-five.listen: Listen to West End Blues (1928). Notice Armstrong's free trumpet introduction at the start: a soloist who takes the stage alone, before the band comes in.

artiest/hot-seven.text:
The Hot Seven was a studio group of trumpeter Louis Armstrong that recorded for the Okeh label in Chicago in 1927. It was an extension of his Hot Five, the band with which he had been recording under his own name since 1925. The core remained largely the same, with Johnny Dodds on clarinet, Lil Hardin Armstrong on piano and Johnny St. Cyr on banjo, among others. Trombonist Kid Ory was in New York at the time and was probably replaced by John Thomas for part of the recordings. A tuba and drums were added, so that the rhythm section sounded fuller.

The best-known recording of the Hot Seven is Potato Head Blues (1927). In it Armstrong plays a solo over short, interrupted chords from the band, so that his trumpet repeatedly stands alone in the space. Other tracks from these sessions are Wild Man Blues and Willie the Weeper.

Together with the Hot Five, the Hot Seven recordings are a turning point in jazz. In the older New Orleans style, trumpet, clarinet and trombone improvised at the same time. On these records the soloist takes the lead, and Armstrong showed how much space a single musician could fill. That shift paved the way for the jazz of the 1930s and later, in which the solo was central.
artiest/hot-seven.listen: Listen to Potato Head Blues (1927). Notice the moment when the band plays only short chords and Armstrong solos through them with his trumpet.

artiest/howard-ashman.text:
Howard Ashman was an American playwright, lyricist and director, born on 17 May 1950 in Baltimore. He began in children's theatre, studied theatre at Goddard College and took a master's degree at Indiana University in 1974. He then worked in New York as an editor and in 1977 became artistic director of the WPA Theater. At a BMI workshop he met the composer Alan Menken. With him he wrote the musical God Bless You, Mr. Rosewater in 1979, and then Little Shop of Horrors, for which Ashman was director, lyricist and librettist. That show became a cult success Off-Broadway and won a Drama Desk Award for best lyrics.

In 1986 Ashman wrote the screenplay for the film version of Little Shop of Horrors, directed by Frank Oz, with two new songs, of which Mean Green Mother from Outer Space received an Oscar nomination. With Menken he then wrote the songs for The Little Mermaid in 1989, Beauty and the Beast and Aladdin for Walt Disney Animation Studios. He is regarded as one of the driving forces behind the Disney Renaissance. In 1992, more than a year after his death, he won the Oscar together with Menken for the song Beauty and the Beast. He died on 14 March 1991 of complications from AIDS.

Ashman brought the dramatic structure of the Broadway musical to the animated film: each song tells you something about what a character wants. That model still determines how many children's films sound.
artiest/howard-ashman.listen: Listen to Under the Sea from The Little Mermaid. Notice how the lyrics are almost a stage number: the song persuades Ariel with arguments, full of rhymes and jokes.

artiest/howard-greenfield.text:
Howard Greenfield was an American lyricist, born on 15 March 1936 in Brooklyn and died on 4 March 1986. In the 1960s he worked out of the Brill Building. As a teenager he got to know Neil Sedaka in his apartment building in Brighton Beach, and by the end of their teens they formed a songwriting duo. Their first recordings were on both sides of The Tokens' debut single in 1956. In 1958 they signed with Aldon Music, owned by Al Nevins and Don Kirshner. In addition, Greenfield had almost simultaneously equally successful partnerships with Jack Keller and Helen Miller.

Greenfield co-wrote four songs that reached number one on the American Billboard chart: Breaking Up Is Hard to Do by Sedaka, Everybody's Somebody's Fool and My Heart Has a Mind of Its Own by Connie Francis, and Love Will Keep Us Together by Captain & Tennille. He also wrote hits for Sedaka, such as Oh! Carol and Calendar Girl, for Connie Francis, for the Everly Brothers with Crying in the Rain, and for the Shirelles. He also wrote the theme songs for television series such as Gidget, Bewitched, The Flying Nun and Hazel.

In 2005 (Is This the Way to) Amarillo, which he wrote with Sedaka in the early 1970s, reached number one in the United Kingdom in the version by Tony Christie from 1971. Greenfield stands for the craftsmanlike Brill Building pop: short songs with lyrics that everyone understands at once.
artiest/howard-greenfield.listen: Listen to Breaking Up Is Hard to Do by Neil Sedaka. Notice the playful lyrics, the rhythm of the singing and how the chorus sticks in your head immediately.

artiest/howard-roberts.text:
Howard Roberts was an American jazz guitarist, teacher and session musician, born on 2 October 1929 in Phoenix, Arizona. He started on guitar at eight, on a student model Gibson that he received for Christmas. At fifteen he was already playing professionally, mainly blues-oriented music, and learned from Black musicians, including trumpeter Art Farmer. He later called that time the most valuable for his development. At seventeen he took a course in the system of Joseph Schillinger, a composer and theorist who applied mathematical principles to art.

In 1950 he moved to Los Angeles, without lodgings and with only a guitar and an amplifier. He played in the after-hours scene with Sonny Stitt, Dexter Gordon and Buddy DeFranco and struck up a friendship with Barney Kessel. Through Jack Marshall he joined Capitol Records in 1963. He worked with Neal Hefti, Henry Mancini, Bobby Troup, Chico Hamilton and George Van Eps. Albums include Jazz Studio Two from 1954, This Is Howard Roberts Color Him Funky from 1963, The Velvet Groove from 1966 and Spinning Wheel from 1969.

Roberts had a style of his own, bluesy and technically strong, and worked a great deal as a studio guitarist. He also taught. He died on 28 June 1992.
artiest/howard-roberts.listen: Listen to This Is Howard Roberts Color Him Funky. Notice the blues feeling in his guitar playing and how loosely he makes the phrases swing.

artiest/howard-rumsey.text:
Howard Rumsey was an American jazz double bassist, born on 7 November 1917 in Brawley, California, and died on 15 July 2015. In the 1950s he led the Lighthouse All-Stars. He began on piano, switched to drums and ended up on bass. He played with Vido Musso and Johnnie Davis, was a member of Stan Kenton's first band, left after an argument and played with Charlie Barnet and Barney Bigard.

In 1949 he was looking for work and found the Lighthouse Club on Pier Avenue in Hermosa Beach. He convinced the owner John Levine to allow jazz and played his first night on 29 May 1949 with immediate success. The first Lighthouse All-Stars consisted of musicians from the Central Avenue scene, including Teddy Edwards, Sonny Criss and Hampton Hawes. The second line-up had Jimmy Giuffre, Shorty Rogers and Shelly Manne and got a contract with Les Koenig's Contemporary Records. In 1953 Rogers, Giuffre and Manne left, and the third line-up consisted of Bud Shank, Bob Cooper, Rolf Ericson and Max Roach.

The Lighthouse All-Stars played every Sunday at the Lighthouse Cafe for almost the entire decade and were one of the most important institutions of modern West Coast jazz. In this way Rumsey gave a home to many Los Angeles musicians.
artiest/howard-rumsey.listen: Listen to a recording by the Lighthouse All-Stars from the 1950s. Notice how relaxed the ensemble sounds and how the horns give each other room.

artiest/howard-shore.text: Howard Shore (born in Toronto in 1946) studied at Berklee and for years was musical director of the television programme Saturday Night Live. His film work began with the director David Cronenberg, with The Brood (1979) and The Fly (1986). There he wrote dark, dissonant music for orchestra. That style also suited thrillers such as The Silence of the Lambs (1991) and Se7en (1995). With The Lord of the Rings (2001–2003) he made the greatest work of his career: a network of dozens of leitmotifs for peoples, places and characters, as in an opera by Wagner. For the trilogy he won three Oscars.
artiest/howard-shore.listen: Notice how each people or place has a tone colour of its own, such as Irish whistle for the hobbits and heavy brass for the enemy.

artiest/howlin-wolf.text:
Howlin' Wolf, born Chester Arthur Burnett, was an American blues singer, guitarist and harmonica player. He was born in 1910 near West Point in Mississippi, grew up in poverty and in the 1930s became a pupil of the Delta blues musician Charley Patton. After a prison sentence and army service he was discovered by Ike Turner, who had him record with producer Sam Phillips in Memphis.

His first record, Moanin' at Midnight (1951), earned him a contract with Chess Records in Chicago. There he played an important part in transforming acoustic Delta blues into electric Chicago blues. Between 1951 and 1969 six of his songs reached the Billboard R&B chart. Well-known songs are Smokestack Lightnin', Little Red Rooster, Killing Floor and Spoonful. His work can be found on albums such as Howlin' Wolf (the so-called Rocking Chair Album) and The London Howlin' Wolf Sessions (1971).

He had a gigantic voice, a raw growl, and an imposing presence. His songs became standards for blues rock and for many later bands. Smokestack Lightning was added to the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999, and in 1991 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He performed until November 1975 and died in January 1976. He is regarded as one of the most influential blues musicians ever.
artiest/howlin-wolf.listen: Listen to Smokestack Lightnin' and notice how the guitar repeats a single riff and how the voice darts between growling, moaning and a high howl. Can you hear the wolf?

artiest/hubei-song-and-dance-ensemble.text:
The Hubei Song and Dance Ensemble is a song and dance company from the Chinese province of Hubei. That province has a rich musical tradition, with its own styles of opera and many folk songs. The company became best known for performances of ancient court music on replicas of instruments from Chinese antiquity.

The occasion was a find in Hubei in the late 1970s: the tomb of Marquis Yi of Zeng, from the fifth century BC. In it lay a large set of bronze bells, a bianzhong, which hung in rows on a wooden rack. Such bells do not sound by means of a clapper, but are struck from the outside with mallets. On recordings from 1989 the company plays pieces such as Bianzhong Chime Bell Solo, Music of the Chu Palace and Concert of the Eight Tones. The name Chu refers to the ancient kingdom in this region. The eight tones are the old Chinese classification of instruments by the material they are made of, such as metal, stone, silk and bamboo.

The music gives an idea of how the court in ancient China may have sounded. It remains a reconstruction, though: nobody knows exactly what was played at the time. Even so, it shows that long before Western pop music there was already complex, organised music, with tuned instruments made specially for the court.
artiest/hubei-song-and-dance-ensemble.listen: Listen to Bianzhong Chime Bell Solo (1989). Notice the clear, resonant sound of the bronze bells and how the notes go on sounding long after they have been struck.

artiest/hubert-rostaing.text:
Hubert Rostaing was a French jazz clarinettist and tenor saxophonist, born on 17 September 1918 in Lyon and died on 10 June 1990 in Paris. He grew up in Algiers, where he learned clarinet and saxophone at the conservatoire and as a teenager performed with the Red Hotters. Later he toured Morocco and Tunisia. After a tour of Luxembourg in 1938 he moved to Paris, and in 1940 he performed in cabaret on the Champs-Élysées.

He joined Django Reinhardt's Quintette du Hot Club de France when Stéphane Grappelli stayed on in London. Alix Combelle passed on his name. He first played saxophone, but switched to clarinet. In 1944 he was voted best clarinettist of the Hot Club in a poll. His playing was influenced by Benny Goodman. He played on and off with Reinhardt until 1948 and made recordings as a bandleader, including with Raymond Legrand, Aimé Barelli and Rex Stewart. With André Hodeir he worked on Autour d'un Récif from 1949 and Saint-Tropez from 1953. He also played rock 'n' roll and classical music.

Later in life he worked as a composer, arranger, conductor and musical director for 53 films and television series. Albums include Le Romantisme from 1976 and the music for the film La baston from 1985. Rostaing shows how the French jazz of the Hot Club flowed into film music.
artiest/hubert-rostaing.listen: Listen to a recording by the Quintette du Hot Club de France from the 1940s. Notice the clarinet alongside Django Reinhardt's guitar, and how smoothly that clarinet carries the melody.

artiest/huelgas-ensemble.text:
The Huelgas Ensemble is a Belgian early-music group, founded in 1971 by the Flemish conductor Paul Van Nevel, who still leads the group. The ensemble consists of singers and instrumentalists and focuses on medieval music from the thirteenth century, Renaissance polyphony and early Baroque, especially of the Franco-Flemish school. The name refers to the Codex Las Huelgas, a manuscript of polyphonic music and one of the most important sources for the thirteenth century.

The discography is large. Early recordings are Las Ensaladas from 1975, Motets Wallons from 1978 and Ars moriendi from 1979. Later came La Favola di Orfeo from 1982, Cypriot Advent Antiphons from 1990 and La Dissection d'un Homme armé, six masses on a Burgundian song, from 1990, among others. In 2009, after eight years with Bernard Coutaz's Harmonia Mundi, the group returned to Sony Classical, which reissued a box of fifteen CDs.

Van Nevel is known for a working method of his own: he often has the singers and himself stand in a large circle and slowly rotate, during concerts and around the microphone in recordings. For a concert in 2005 at the Rheingau Musik Festival, the pews had to be unbolted from the floor of the basilica for this. The ensemble is one of the groups that made the polyphony of before Bach audible again.
artiest/huelgas-ensemble.listen: Listen to La Dissection d'un Homme armé. Notice how the same familiar melody emerges again and again in different masses, surrounded by other voices.
